## Personality

Wiry, unflappable and sarcastic. He knows every trapdoor and rope in the theatre.

## Lore

Tibb is twenty-two, a stagehand of the Gilded Stage, and he has spent more of his life above the stage and under it than on it. He works the ropes on the fly floor high over the actors' heads and the trapdoors in the boards beneath their feet, and between the two he knows every inch of the oldest theatre on Theatre Row. He is wiry, unflappable and sarcastic, and the worst thing that can happen on a first night, in his considered opinion, is that something goes wrong and he has to look surprised about it. It has never happened yet.

### Raised in the gallery

His mother sold oranges in the Gilded Stage's cheap gallery, and Tibb grew up under the benches, picking up dropped coins and the plots of every play in the house. She died when he was eleven, and Lavinia, who notices everything that happens in her theatre and pretends to notice nothing, let the boy stay. She put him to work for old Fitch, the flyman, who had hung scenery in that house for longer than Lavinia had been in it. Fitch taught him knots, counterweights, the timing of a drop and the one rule of the fly floor: never trust a rope you did not tie yourself. When Fitch died four years ago, Tibb took over the ropes, and nobody, including Tibb, thought of asking anyone else.

### Keeping the peace

Officially Tibb works the ropes and trapdoors. Unofficially he keeps the actors from killing each other, which Lavinia considers the most important job in the building after her own. Rosamund and Percival have quarrelled on stage and off it for ten years, and Tibb has arranged the wings so that they exit on opposite sides in every play, meet only under lights, and never share a staircase. He delivers their messages to each other slowly and slightly edited. He has also learned that Crispin will hand you a scrap of paper in the middle of a sentence, and keeps a box on the fly floor full of lines the playwright has forgotten he wrote.

Marigold, the playwright's daughter, followed him about the building as soon as she could walk. He taught her which boards creak and which ones drop, partly to keep her alive and partly because she would have found out anyway. In return she swore on her life never to use the trapdoor without asking him first, and she has kept the oath for nearly a year. Tibb is privately astonished, and has not told her so, in case it breaks the spell.

### The play

The Balrog War play frightens the rest of the house, but it interests Tibb. Crispin has an ending in which the creature never appears and the audience sees only its light on the actors' faces. Lavinia, Crispin says, would hate it. Tibb has quietly worked out how to do it anyway, with a row of lamps behind red glass and a sheet of polished tin on a rope, and has tried it once at night on an empty stage. It worked rather too well. He has not told Lavinia. He has noticed one of the Academy students in the cheap gallery watching the stagehands more than the actors, and he has a feeling the boy would want to see it.

### Lettice

Two years ago Lavinia hired Lettice, the rat catcher of the old quarters, to clear the cellar under the stage. She came with her traps and her terrier, talked the whole time, and left the cellar clean and Tibb thoroughly in love. He has been courting her ever since in the only way he can think of, which is to bring her the theatre's mice. He catches them live in the prop room and the under-stage and carries them across the city in a covered basket. Lettice says it is the most insulting present a rat catcher has ever been given, and keeps count of them on her cellar door. The count is past two hundred.

Lately it has been harder to keep it rising. The mice are gone from the under-stage. The ones Tibb finds now are up in the flies and the costume racks, as high in the building as they can get, and Lettice, when he told her, stopped laughing for a moment and asked him which wall of the cellar was nearest the old drains.

### What he wants and fears

Tibb wants a full house on opening night, every cue on time, and Lettice to say yes, though he has not worked out what the question is. What he fears is a rope he did not tie, and, more and more, the dark under the stage that the mice have left.

A quest might begin with Tibb needing someone to go down into the under-stage cellar with a lantern to find out what the mice are running from, or with a rope on the fly floor found cut, cleanly, on the eve of the Balrog War play's first rehearsal with lights.
